assertion: USDA's November 2026 WASDE reflected strong yields — corn at 179.6 bushels per acre and soybeans at a record 53.3 — yet season-average farm prices sit near $4.60 for corn and $12.10 for soybeans.
measure: WASDE corn yield per acre season-average farm price

assertion: University of Illinois farmdoc budgets put full-cost corn breakevens (including typical cash rent) in the $4.90–$5.20 range on northern and central Illinois land and higher farther south; soybean breakevens run roughly $11–$11.60.
inaccuracy: The article says $4.90-$5.20 for northern/central Illinois corn; farmdoc says just below $5, and soybeans $11.10-$11.28 rather than up to $11.60. Figures are 2027 budgets.

assertion: With full-cost corn breakevens clustering in the $4.80–$5.20 range and soybeans near $11–$12, every additional dollar of fertilizer or diesel has a clearer opportunity cost.
source_finding: farmdoc: just below $5 to $5.39 corn; $11.10 to nearly $12 soy
inaccuracy: The article gives $4.80 as the low end here and $4.90 earlier; farmdoc's lowest corn figure is just below $5.

assertion: Early-November retail surveys showed anhydrous ammonia near $1,003 per ton (up roughly 17% year-over-year) and urea around $662 (up about 11%).
Steady yields are rolling in again this harvest, but the old habit of pouring on more fertilizer and fuel to chase every last bushel of production is losing its appeal.
source_finding: WASDE: corn 179.6 (down 1.6 from October, 186.5 in 2025/26); soybeans 53.3 record
inaccuracy: The article says yields are steady and strong; USDA cut the corn yield 1.6 bu from October and it is 6.9 bu below 2025/26, though soybean yield is a record.
measure: WASDE corn yield per acre season-average farm price
